body:
Worth double-checking whether the new setup produces the same results as the old one....

In general, my feeling is that in an ideal world calling a callback would use the global of that callable as the entry settings thing, so calling a callback doesn't require passing in external state.  This requires that all callables have an associated global, though.  That's true for functions, and and IDL-defined objects with `[[Call]]`, but there are some ES built-in objects (e..g the return value of `Function.prototype.bind`, apparently!) that don't have an associated global right now.  Maybe they should.

Also, a related issue is that https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#runtime-script-errors-in-documents assumes there is a script, which is not the case for a builtin function, bound or not, being called directly as a callback.  I thought this used to be defined more clearly in a way that worked for all callables, but I might have been confused.

> In particular, I don't see how propagating it across Web IDL callbacks works. Think things like:
> 
> ``` js
> setTimeout(someWindow.postMessage.bind(someWindow, stuff), 0);
> ```
> 
> and what the incumbent settings object will be when postMessage is invoked. What will it be with the spec as it's written right now.

It looks like the bug here is that bound functions are not created with a ScriptOrModule. They should be created with the current execution context's ScriptOrModule. I can PR ES to fix that. If that gets fixed then step 2 of [GetActiveScriptOrModule()](https://tc39.github.io/ecma262/#sec-getactivescriptormodule) will return the bound function's execution context.

Did you have something else in mind though?

> I assume the entry settings object in this case will be something sane-ish, in that it will be associated with the Function that is the return value of bind in this case, right?

This is unclear to me because IDL's "invoke" (which is what setTimeout references) is has not been up to date with HTML for a long time (way before my changes). It's unclear whether it uses "prepare to run a callback" and "clean up after running a callback". I guess if we fixed IDL it would:
- Accept the bound function
- Convert it to an IDL callback type whose "callback context" was the bound function's ScriptOrModule component's settings object
- When it's time to invoke the IDL callback type, prepare to run a callback using the "callback context" (and clean up with the same callback context afterward).

In that case yes the entry settings object would be the settings object of the bound function. Which I believe would be the same as the incumbent per my above reasoning.

> Oh, and importantly are there ever JavaScript execution contexts that do not have a script or a module associated with them? If not, why not? What is the ScriptOrModule when the callback function is called in the case above?

The intent was that only the very top-level contexts, which are basically a spec artifact, should be missing ScriptOrModule. You found a bug for bound functions, but otherwise it should be the case always.

> Digging into the ES end of this a bit more, builtin functions have [[ScriptOrModule]] set to null, afaict. See https://tc39.github.io/ecma262/#sec-createbuiltinfunction

Right. The idea is that when digging up the stack for the closest ScriptOrModule you have to skip over built-in functions.

> As far as entry settings objects... I'm not sure what "the script corresponding to the running execution context" is in the EnqueueJob section in the HTML spec. Why would there be such a script at all? See builtin functions above.

That was supposed to link to https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#script-corresponding-to-the-running-execution-context. I have no idea why it does not :(. As explained above though there should always be such a script.

> Also, a related issue is that https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#runtime-script-errors-in-documents assumes there is a script, which is not the case for a builtin function, bound or not, being called directly as a callback.

I think this has always been that way :-/.

The commit message for https://github.com/tc39/ecma262/commit/698819cbf1d79a58532a66ecfe5feaca67cb3112 gives details on how every execution context is supposed to get a ScriptOrModule. (There is a level above the top-level, which is the spec artifact I alluded to; the commit message doesn't mention those.) As you can see determining an execution context's ScriptOrModule often relies on determining some relevant function's [[ScriptOrModule]]. That is why bound functions not having [[ScriptOrModule]] breaks things.

Even in the case of a built-in calling a built-in, as long as Web IDL's "invoke" uses https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#prepare-to-run-a-callback, step 4 will ensure that there is a Script-correlated execution context on the stack.

Upon trying to fix bound functions I see that they're not actually broken. They don't even create an execution context when called or constructed, they just delegate to the original function. So they don't need [[ScriptOrModule]]. The execution context that executes will just be the execution context of the normal function.

So, bound built-in functions have the problem to the same extent as other built-in functions do.

With this in mind my above ideas for updating IDL seem wrong. I guess it needs to be more like:
1. Accept a function argument _f_ and convert it to a IDL callback _c_
2. If _f_ has a [[ScriptOrModule]] internal slot whose value is not null, let _c_'s call context be _f_.[[ScriptOrModule]].[[HostDefined]]'s settings object.
3. If _f_ is a bound function exotic object, whose [[BoundTargetFunction]] has a [[ScriptOrModule]] internal slot whose value is not null, let _c_'s call context be _f_.[[BoundTargetFunction]].[[ScriptOrModule]].[[HostDefined]]'s settings object.
4. Otherwise, let _c_'s call context be the ... entry settings object? not sure

Then when you invoke _c_ you prepare to run a callback using _c_'s call context and cleanup using the same.

@domenic Could you stop, back up, for a second, and describe the actual behavior you're trying to achieve?  There are three relevant things to consider when making a call to a callback, I believe:
1.  Where exceptions will get reported (i.e. which window will get error events fired at it).
2.  What the entry settings object ends up being.
3.  What the incumbent settings object ends up being if the callback is a builtin function (possibly bound).  This is the only case in which it matters, because if callback is what ES6 calls an "ECMAScript Function Object" then it will have associated ES code which will then end up providing the incumbent settings object for anything that code calls.  This might be able to go away if we get rid of incumbent settings objects, of course.

Last time this was all discussed, I believe we all agreed on the following behavior, which was then implemented in Gecko, attempted to be implemented in the HTML spec, and at least bugs filed on the IDL spec:
1.  When calling a callback, exceptions get reported to the global of that callback.  This requires that every callable have an associated global, which we believed to be the case; I now realize that this is not the case for the return value of `Function.prototype.bind`.  But we could fix that, if we wanted to: just store the current `Realm` when creating the bound function object.  There were some longish threads about this aspect of the behavior.
2.  When calling a callback, the entry settings object is the settings object corresponding to the global of that callback.  Again, this assumes that every callable has an associated global.
3.  When calling a callback, the incumbent settings object is set to the value it had when the conversion to an IDL callback happened (so that doing `setTimeout(foo.bind(stuff))` is equivalent to just calling foo directly.  The IDL spec was in fact updated to do this.

Note that this setup means that when you want to run a callback you don't need to cart around any state except the callback itself: the entry settings object is deduced from the callable, and the incumbent settings object is captured by the callback creation.  In particular, "prepare to run a callback" does not need an environment settings object as input as far as I can tell if this is the setup being implemented.

Now, are you aiming for this behavior?  If not, can you describe the behavior you _are_ aiming for and point to where it was discussed and decided to switch to this other behavior?

I am definitely aiming for that behavior! I was just trying to update it to work with ES6, and in the process it seemed much nicer if we could just phrase things in terms of the ES execution context (I think you mentioned this in a thread a while back). So there was some significant refactoring. I hope the end result ends up simpler than before, and requires less monkeypatching of ES; that is the goal. Not any normative changes.

I can see how the scheme you describe, of going from callback -> Realm -> settings object, will be simpler for calling IDL callbacks. I'm not sure how to integrate it with the definitions of incumbent and entry settings object that also work in other situations (like calling functions which are not converted to IDL callbacks, or at the various points in the spec where we "jump to a code entry-point" for a script, or in eval contexts, or similar).

> In particular, "prepare to run a callback" does not need an environment settings object as input as far as I can tell if this is the setup being implemented.

Prepare to run a callback has always taken a settings object in order to mark it as a candidate entry settings object. Do you have a different way of determining entry settings objects, than marking them during this step? I don't see how it's avoidable for scripts that are not IDL callbacks or JS function objects (like setTimeout strings or `<script>` contents). So I think that algorithm still needs to take a settings object, and for IDL callbacks it can just get that settings object via callback -> Realm -> settings object

OK, good, we agree on the goals (including trying to do this in terms of ES execution contexts).  Just wanted to double-check that before I continue digging into details.

Good point about calling functions that are not IDL callbacks.  That needs to set up an entry settings object, of course, and may need some sort of "capture the incumbent settings object" thing like IDL callbacks, for similar reasons.  I _think_ the only really relevant case here is `Promise` callback functions, since that's the only async function execution in ES proper right now.  They're implemented as IDL callbacks in Gecko at the moment, so I hadn't thought it through; my apologies.  And yes, running `setTimeout` strings or toplevel scripts does require passing in the relevant settings object, I agree.  Maybe "prepare to run a callback" needs renaming, if its primary purpose in life isn't really about callbacks...

Anyway, now I understand why Hixie kept saying that settings objects were in a many to one relationship with globals.  In his setup, you had to have settings objects for the same global some of which were marked as entry settings objects and some were not.

Specifically, consider the situation in which you do something like:

```
setTimeout(someFunc, 0);
```

and `someFunc` fires an event, and one of the event listeners calls `someFunc` which this time calls some API that needs to find the entry settings object.  That should be the thing associated with the running event listener, not the one associated with `someFunc`, which implies that we need two different things associated with `someFunc` somehow: one for its invocation via `setTimeout` and a different one for the call from the event listener.

So in the new world, we have two separate "JavaScript execution context"s here for the two invocations of `someFunc`, right?  That's good.  But they share a single `ScriptOrModule`, don't they?  So we can't really hang entry settings stuff off of the `ScriptOrModule`, unless I'm missing something.

> I think the only really relevant case here is Promise callback functions, since that's the only async function execution in ES proper right now.

I think I agree. Currently this is taken care of by https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#enqueuejob(queuename,-job,-arguments) which does the prepare/cleanup steps before/after running the job.

> Maybe "prepare to run a callback" needs renaming, if its primary purpose in life isn't really about callbacks...

Yeah I agree with this as well. In #443 I will rename it to "prepare to run a script" since I am making changes in those areas anyway.

>  In his setup, you had to have settings objects for the same global some of which were marked as entry settings objects and some were not.

Oh dear. Looking things over, I broke this. Previously there was a stack of settings objects and you could mark entries in the stack as candidate entry settings object. I always interpreted this as the stack being of { settings object, is candidate entry settings object } pairs, so you could mark entries in the stack independent of marking the settings objects themselves. But in the current spec (i.e. after my recent refactor) it seems like it has just collapsed to "Label _settings_ as a candidate entry settings object", which is not good.

I think we should maintain the 1:1 settings object to global correspondence. It seems like the best approach is to mark JavaScript execution contexts as "candidate entry execution contexts". (From an execution context you can go execution context -> ScriptOrModule -> HTML "script" -> script's settings object.)

> Specifically, consider the situation in which you do something like:

To make sure I am following: at what points in the previous spec do "candidate entry settings object" get marked? I am thinking they get marked in the IDL "Invoke" inside setTimeout's task, and the IDL "Invoke" inside dispatchEvent? Would you mind spelling this out in a bit more detail, preferably calling out which code lives in a different iframe or whatever so that we have two clearly distinct settings objects.

> I always interpreted this as the stack being of { settings object, is candidate entry settings object } pairs

Yeah, that would work too.

> I think we should maintain the 1:1 settings object to global correspondence.

Worksforme, if we can manage it (i.e. if we never end up with different responsible browsing contexts or whatnot given a global)!

> It seems like the best approach is to mark JavaScript execution contexts as "candidate entry execution contexts"

That makes sense, yes.

> I am thinking they get marked in the IDL "Invoke" inside setTimeout's task, and the IDL "Invoke" inside dispatchEvent?

Yes, that was my understanding too.

In my example, the idea was that `someFunc` lives in one global and the event listener that calls it lives in a different global.  I think marking the entry settings bit on the JS execution context will make this work as expected, as long as we can go from whatever execution context we set up for an IDL "invoke" or Promise job to a settings object (i.e. it's not just the execution context for a builtin function invocation, but something else we set up separately).

OK, I think we have a plan, although the details of how I'm going to fix this are a little unclear--- I started typing them then confused myself. I think it will work itself out when I actually go to do the work, which I need to delay until after #443. I'll report back soon.
Accidentally closed by my wording in https://github.com/whatwg/html/commit/0866f1b3f4b4ea5a99a30909e9bbe557dea0b460 ("does not yet fix" was seen by GitHub as "fix").

OK, I have cleared enough off my plate that I can make this my highest priority. @bzbarsky, if you would be OK paging this stuff back in, here is my current plan for entry settings object:
- As previously straightened out, we have 1:1:1 globals/Realms/settings objects
- The _settings object of an execution context_ is defined as the settings object corresponding to the execution context's [[Realm]].
  - This is a simplification of the current definition which indirects through [[ScriptOrModule]].
- All execution contexts get associated with them a boolean flag, "is candidate entry execution context".
- The entry execution context is the topmost entry in the execution context stack whose "is candidate entry execution context" flag is set.
- The entry settings object is the settings object of the entry execution context.

What remains is to ensure that we tag the appropriate execution contexts as candidates at all times. The mechanism for doing so is as follows:
- Every Realm/settings object/global has a top-level "realm execution context" which is created when creating the Realm.
  - This is mainly used for running code without a naturally-associated execution context, such as `<script>` or `setTimeout` strings or similar.
  - However, as discussed below, we also want to use it in cases where there is a natural execution context, such as running JS functions, since it helps us track entry settings objects.
- Breakdown by way of calling author script:
  - Run a classic script/run a module script (takes as argument a script _s_)
    - Tags/untags _s_'s settings object's realm execution context as a candidate before/after compiling and running the script
    - Pushes/pops that execution context before/after compiling and running the script
  - IDL invoke of author callbacks (takes as argument a JS callable _c_)
    - Tags/untags GetFunctionRealm(_c_)'s settings object's realm execution context as a candidate before/after doing the JS Call()
      - Note that GetFunctionRealm() handles bound functions and proxies for us
    - Pushes/pops that execution context before/after doing the JS Call().
  - Promise callbacks, via EnqueueJob (takes as argument a PendingJob Record _j_)
    - Tags/untags _j_.[[Realm]]'s settings object's realm execution context as a candidate before/after running the JS abstract operation given by _j_.[[Job]]
    - Pushes/pops that execution context before/after running the JS abstract operation given by to _j_.[[Job]]
  - Direct calls to author code (e.g. structured clone's _input_.[[GetOwnProperty]](key))
    - Requires more case-by-case work; see #855 
    - Postponed for now; tackle that next

This is a little roundabout---the frequent realm -> settings object -> realm execution context dance during the marking phase seems a bit silly, especially since we later go execution context -> realm -> settings object to get back "entry settings object". But I am pretty sure it is necessary if we want JavaScript to maintain the stack for us, since it is JavaScript's execution context stack that is the real stack in play here.

@domenic So thinking about https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/473#issuecomment-212164549 I have the following questions:
1. Do we know whether JS implementations in fact have an execution context stack?  Certainly Gecko actually implements a settings object stack and afaik SpiderMonkey has no concept of an execution context stack.  Maybe this doesn't matter because the behavior is not observably different and this is all a specification device?
2. When you say "tag as a candidate" is that an irreversible operation (I see no untagging in your steps above)?  That is, can we effectively pretend that all realm execution contexts are candidates all the time?  If not, is the difference observable, and if so how?
3.  Do we know what engines do right now for the Proxy case, and particularly when the Proxy constructor from one Realm (call it R1) is called with a function target from another Realm (call it R2)?  I believe that if such a Proxy is then used in a Web IDL callback then Gecko will currently use R1 as the entry Realm/global/etc, though we can probably try to change that if needed.  It's not clear to me whether there's a principled solution here, though it does make some sense for a Proxy to a function to trigger onerror on the same window as the function would...

As far as direct calls to author code go, Gecko handles those by requiring that all such calls be preceded by effectively selecting the global you think you're operating in, which in your terms would mark that global's Realm's realm execution context as an entry candidate and push it on the stack.

Also, is my understanding correct that if we have this setup in place, then popping an entry candidate execution context off the stack is precisely when you report uncaught exceptions?

> Do we know whether JS implementations in fact have an execution context stack?

That's a good question. I certainly assume all implementations have some kind of execution stack concept, but I'm not sure how well it maps to spec-level execution contexts.

I  think in the end it doesn't matter, since it's a spec device. It's a little worrying that this moves the spec's model further away from Gecko's though...

> When you say "tag as a candidate" is that an irreversible operation (I see no untagging in your steps above)?

This was imprecise. Basically every push should be "push + tag" and every pop should be "pop + untag". #1091 takes care of this in more detail (for the run a classic/module script case and EnqueueJob case); see https://github.com/whatwg/html/pull/1091/files#diff-36cd38f49b9afa08222c0dc9ebfe35ebR87451). I will edit that description to be more precise.

> Do we know what engines do right now for the Proxy case, and particularly when the Proxy constructor from one Realm (call it R1) is called with a function target from another Realm (call it R2)? I believe that if such a Proxy is then used in a Web IDL callback then Gecko will currently use R1 as the entry Realm/global/etc, though we can probably try to change that if needed.

I haven't investigated engine behavior here. I think R2 is more correct according to the ES spec authors, because GetFunctionRealm() will return R2. The same logic applies to bound functions, if you use the Function.prototype.bind from R1 on a function from R2. I'm not sure if they had any principles in mind when deciding how GetFunctionRealm() operates, besides perhaps the misguided notion that "only real functions have realm internal slots" or something.

> As far as direct calls to author code go, Gecko handles those by requiring that all such calls be preceded by effectively selecting the global you think you're operating in, which in your terms would mark that global's Realm's realm execution context as an entry candidate and push it on the stack.

Yeah, I think I would spec this as doing "prepare to run script" / "clean up after running script" before/after calling author code.

> Also, is my understanding correct that if we have this setup in place, then popping an entry candidate execution context off the stack is precisely when you report uncaught exceptions?

Yes. In "run a classic script", the error reporting step is immediately followed by the "clean up after running script" step. The latter is the one that pops the entry candidate execution context. I am not sure if the relative ordering between these two steps is observable, but I believe it's always been report, then pop/un-mark, even in the old days.

> but I'm not sure how well it maps to spec-level execution contexts

SpiderMonkey's, not at all.  In particular, it only has entries for actual running scripts or functions on it; it can't represent the "we aren't running anything yet, but have a thing on the stack" state.

I agree about the worrying thing, insofar as it means there is extra work involved in figuring out whether the same results are produced in all the edge cases.  But I _think_ Gecko's setup will be OK here, actually.

> Basically every push should be "push + tag" and every pop should be "pop + untag".

Pop+untag is _definitely_ wrong unless "untag" means "restore the old state, which may be true or false".  Consider running a `<script>` which creates and inserts an inline `<script>`.  When that inline script executes (sync) it will tag their (shared) Realm's realm execution context (or am I totally confused here?), then if it untags when it's done and we return to the first `<script>` we were running... we should still have its realm execution context tagged, right?

> besides perhaps the misguided notion that "only real functions have realm internal slots" 

Not sure about misguided, but I think that was the driving notion, yes.

> I am not sure if the relative ordering between these two steps is observable

Pretty sure it's not, since the reporting steps should not be doing anything sync....

> Pop+untag is definitely wrong unless "untag" means "restore the old state, which may be true or false". 

Good catch, thanks. You're right that simply untagging doesn't work here, just as the spec's current wording doesn't work as we discussed upthread in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/473#issuecomment-170104623.

I see three solutions, the first of which is the minimal modification and the other two I wanted to mention to make sure we understand all our options:
- (A) Change the execution context's "is candidate entry execution context" flag to a "entrance counter" or similarly-named thing. On pushing, increment the counter; on popping, decrement it. If the counter is > 0, it's a candidate.
- (B) Go back to maintaining a stack of { settings object, is candidate entry } pairs and stop trying to piggyback on the execution context stack. Would involve adding more hooks to ES. Would match Firefox's implementation, I assume. This would be like the old spec, but more explicit.
- (C) Assume and/or verify that I can use the ScriptOrModule mechanisms I added to ES to correctly define incumbent settings object. (Maybe the spec's current definition is correct, or correct modulo some bound function/proxy edge cases. I haven't yet checked, as I was hoping to fix entry first then work on incumbent.) If that's the case, we don't actually need a stack of all settings objects, where some of them are tagged as candidate-entry. We can just keep a stack of candidate entry settings objects, and the topmost entry on the stack is the entry settings object.

Right now I'd tend toward option (A), but it might be out of inertia. If you think the idea of using the ES execution context stack is turning out to be nice in theory but in practice a failure, and I should pull back and start working on options (B) or (C), let me know.

Solution (A) is basically the same as "set to true, then set to whatever the old value was", right.

Solution (B) means we have to maintain our stack on function calls, which is what we're trying to sort of avoid, right?  I don't think it matches Firefox all that closely.  Basically, Firefox does the following:
- Entry settings objects are maintained entirely via a stack that lives outside the JS engine.  JS execution never affect the entry settings stack anyway, because the only times something can change the entry settings object is when the UA is calling into JS, so we can just handle it in Gecko, outside JS.  Promises are handled by having Gecko control calling into them, which is needed anyway because Gecko is what has the event loop.
- Incumbent settings objects are handled via a split approach.  There's an out-of-band stack that gets things pushed on it whenever an entry settings thing is pushed.  It also gets things pushed on it when we push explicit incumbent globals for things like IDL callbacks.  When something gets pushed on the incumbent stack, we set a "ignore" bit on the currently active JS stack frame, if any; when it gets popped it unsets the bit.  When we want to determine the incumbent global, we consult the JS stack.  If that's empty, or if the top frame on it has the "ignore" bit set, we use the incumbent global stack; otherwise we use the Realm of the top thing on the JS stack.

We happen to use a single stack for the entry and out-of-band incumbent stacks, with booleans labeling the entry settings bits, because that's what the spec used to do.  But conceptually, they're really totally separate stacks, right?

Solution (C) is hard to envision for me given the need for explicit pushing of particular incumbent settings in some situations.  We really do need to be able to push some things that don't correspond to any executing JS yet to capture that.

So Solution (A) is probably fine. I think.  Unless we want to just go ahead and create altogether separate stacks for incumbent and entry stuff; the former would reuse the JS execution context stack and the latter would not.  Some places would need to push onto both stacks.

The one thing that does need double-checking with solution (A) is that we can never have a situation in which a "realm execution context" is topmost on the stack but should NOT be considered the entry thing.  Because obviously you can't control what's up-stack from you and it might have incremented the counter on that realm execution context already.  Seems to me like the "realm execution context" is topmost only if we're not running script or running a toplevel script or setTimeout-with-string thing and have not called any functions, and in all those cases it should in fact be the entry thing....

OK, I'm happy with solution (A) for now, and added that to #1091. It's possible that in the future we may evolve toward

>  Unless we want to just go ahead and create altogether separate stacks for incumbent and entry stuff; the former would reuse the JS execution context stack and the latter would not. Some places would need to push onto both stacks.

as I work to fix incumbent, but I think it'd be unlikely, especially if you say (B) doesn't match things in Gecko.

> We happen to use a single stack for the entry and out-of-band incumbent stacks, with booleans labeling the entry settings bits, because that's what the spec used to do. But conceptually, they're really totally separate stacks, right?

I think so, although it's possible they are both "subsets" of the JavaScript execution context stack.

> The one thing that does need double-checking with solution (A) is that we can never have a situation in which a "realm execution context" is topmost on the stack but should NOT be considered the entry thing.

I think we're safe, as you say. The places the "realm execution context" are pushed are enumerated pretty clearly: clicking the dfn.js panel for "realm execution context" will find them all. (I've verified ES doesn't use the concept itself in any sneaky way.)
Should we mention that assumption around realm execution context somewhere?

Well, we already say

> When we run a classic script or run a module script, this execution context becomes the top of the JavaScript execution context stack, on top of which another execution context specific to the script in question is pushed.

I guess we could add a sentence like "These are the only times this execution context is pushed," but it doesn't really seem necessary...

OK, now let's look at incumbent. I think the spec's current definition is conceptually sound. To summarize it schematically:
- Make sure all user-defined functions have an associated "script" (#concept-script)
- Look at the execution context stack to find the topmost function that has an associated script
- That script's settings object is then the incumbent settings object

This is a bit different than the model you seem to have in mind, e.g. in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/473#issuecomment-169856378, which seems roughly to be based on the idea of "setting" the incumbent settings object to something, and "capturing" an appropriate settings object at IDL callback creation which will later help with "setting" it during invocation. I think the models are equivalent equivalent, though, and IMO the spec's current one nicely matches the rough description given in the spec for the incumbent concept:

> This corresponds to the most-recently-entered author function or script on the stack.

---

Now for the details.

The spec's current definition seems to be obviously right if you don't involve bound functions/proxies, or the top level of script (where there are no functions to be concerned with). Promise callbacks, in particular, seem to work fine (as long as they are not bound functions or proxies).

**The top level:**

The top level seems a bit broken right now. E.g. in the simple case of

``` js
<script>
window.someAPIThatUsesIncumbentSettingsObject();
</script>
```

I believe we reach step 5 of https://tc39.github.io/ecma262/#sec-getactivescriptormodule and the assert fails, since the topmost execution context is (because of "prepare to run a script") the "realm execution context", which has no ScriptOrModule component---it's shared by all scripts in the realm.

I'm not sure exactly what the correct fix is here, but it doesn't seem that hard. I at first wrote down a few ideas but they don't seem bulletproof yet so I'll think on it a bit more.

**Bound functions and proxies:**

I think the way to do this is to define GetFunctionScriptOrModule(), similar to GetFunctionRealm(), which simply pierces bound functions and proxies in a similar manner. With that in hand, and modifying GetActiveScriptOrModule to make use of it, I think everything just works.

NOTE! One might momentarily think, "why not just use GetFunctionRealm()? Once we get the script, we're just going to grab it's settings object (= realm) anyway". But this will not work, because functions like, say, setTimeout or %Promise%.prototype.then all have realms. They just don't have scripts!

---

Would love your thoughts on the above.

What does the "Look at the execution context stack to find the topmost function that has an associated script" thing do when built-in functions are involved?

Specifically, if you do `setTimeout(someBuiltinFunction)` what will the incumbent global be when `someBuiltinFunction` is invoked?  The idea of the "capture and set" approach is that it should be whatever the incumbent global was when `setTimeout` was invoked, so you can't change around the incumbent global by invoking things async.

Here is the concrete proposal.

#### New operation: GetFunctionScriptOrModule()
- Most of the time returns the function's [[ScriptOrModule]].
- If a proxy or bound function, pierces to return the target's.
- Built-in functions always have null [[ScriptOrModule]] and so return null.

#### New version of GetActiveScriptScriptOrModule()
1. If the execution context stack is empty, return null.
2. Let _ec_ be the topmost execution context on the execution context stack for which GetFunctionScriptOrModule(the execution context's Function component) is not null.
3. If such an execution context exists, return GetActiveScriptOrModule(_ec_).
4. Return null.

#### New definition of incumbent settings object
1. Let _scriptOrModule_ be the result of JavaScript's GetActiveScriptOrModule() abstract operation.
2. If _scriptOrModule_ is null, return the entry settings object.
3. Return the settings object of the script in _scriptOrModule_'s [[HostDefined]] field.

#### How this handles the tricky case

The case in question is

``` html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<iframe></iframe>
<script>
  window.setTimeout(frames[0].postMessage.bind(frames[0], "x", "*"));
</script>
```

The question is: what is the incumbent settings object referred to by the `postMessage` algorithm? It should be `window`'s settings object, not `frames[0]`'s.

In this case GetActiveScriptOrModule() returns null: there are no functions with non-null [[ScriptOrModule]] values in the execution context stack.

So we fall through to step 2, and return the entry settings object: which is `window`.

I see. Thanks, I am now convinced that we need to store the incumbent settings object on conversion to an IDL callback type. We can use IDL's "callback context" for this; currently it stores the "incumbent script" which I believe has not been a concept since before I started editing.

#### New concept: the backup incumbent settings object stack

This is a new stack associated with each event loop.

#### IDL modifications
- Update the conversion of JS values implementing interfaces to store the incumbent settings object in the IDL value's callback context.
- "Invoke" and friends get modified to push/pop the callback's callback context onto the backup incumbent settings object stack.

#### HTML modifications
- In prepare to run script/clean up after running script, push/pop the realm execution context's settings object onto the backup incumbent settings object stack.
- I believe this only impacts cases like `<!DOCTYPE html><script>window.somethingThatUsesIncumbentSettingsObject()</script>` and other ways of running top-level script like `javascript:` URLs.

#### New definition of incumbent settings object
1. Let _scriptOrModule_ be the result of JavaScript's GetActiveScriptOrModule() abstract operation.
2. If _scriptOrModule_ is null, return the topmost entry in the backup incumbent settings object stack.
3. Return the settings object of the script in _scriptOrModule_'s [[HostDefined]] field.

#### How this handles the tricky case

``` html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<iframe></iframe>
<script>
  window.setTimeout(frames[0].postMessage.bind(frames[0], "x", "*"));
</script>
```

Upon calling setTimeout:
- The incumbent settings object is that of `window`
- We store the IDL callback `{ jsFunction: <the result of .bind>, callbackContext: <window's settings object> }`

Inside the task posted by setTimeout:
- We IDL-invoke the stored IDL callback.
- This pushes the settings object of `window` onto the backup incumbent settings object stack.

Inside the postMessage algorithm:
- We ask for the incumbent settings object.
- GetActiveScriptOrModule() returns null.
- We fall back to the backup incumbent settings object stack, returning the settings object of `window`.

That approach is basically what hixie's spec was aiming at, I believe.  You're right that it's pretty much identical to the Firefox implementation; the one difference is that in Firefox the "global script" case is represented by the equivalent of the execution context stack because we have a way of getting directly from a JS stackframe, including a global one, to a corresponding global.  So we only use the backup stack for the saved incumbent thing.

One other issue that probably needs addressing: the setup described in https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/473#issuecomment-216683695 only affects IDL callbacks.  We should at least think about what happens with promise callbacks.  Ideally those would do the same thing (capture the incumbent settings at the point of the `then()` call, push it onto the backup stack before invoking the callback).
